label: Charge, current, voltage and power
prereqs: Derivative as slope of tangent line
lesson:
# Charge, current, voltage and power

Every number a circuit simulator, timer or power tool reports is built from four quantities: charge, current, voltage and power. Current is charge in motion, voltage is energy per unit charge, and power is their product. A tool designer meets them everywhere: switching energy in power analysis, charge delivered by a driver in timing, dissipation in electromigration and IR-drop checks. Getting the units and the integrals right is the first step to trusting any engine's output.

## Current as the rate of charge flow

Current is the rate at which charge crosses a surface, $i(t) = dq/dt$. Turning that around, the charge delivered between two times is the integral of current, $q = \int i\,dt$: the area under the current waveform. A constant current $I$ for a time $T$ delivers $IT$. A current that ramps linearly from 0 to $I$ over $T$ delivers half of that, the area of a triangle, $IT/2$.

Units scale conveniently on chips: one milliampere flowing for one nanosecond moves one picocoulomb. Example: a driver whose current ramps from 0 to 20 mA over 4 ns delivers $20 \cdot 4/2 = 40$ pC. If that charge lands on a 10 pF load it raises the load by $Q/C = 4$ V. A simulator integrates exactly this relation at every node and every time step.

## Voltage, energy and power

Voltage is energy per unit charge: moving charge $q$ through a potential difference $V$ exchanges energy $qV$. Power is the rate of that exchange, $p = dw/dt = v\,i$. For a steady supply voltage and current, energy over an interval is simply $E = VIt$.

Example: a block draws a steady 25 mA from a 1.2 V supply for 10 ns. Its power is $1.2 \cdot 25 = 30$ mW, and the energy taken is $30 \text{ mW} \times 10 \text{ ns} = 300$ pJ (one milliwatt for one nanosecond is one picojoule). Power-analysis engines sum exactly these products over every supply pin and time window. The sign convention matters: with current entering the positive terminal of an element, positive $vi$ means the element absorbs power, and negative means it delivers power, as a source does.

## Power dissipated in a resistor

For a resistor, Ohm's law $v = iR$ turns $p = vi$ into two equivalent forms: $p = i^2 R$ and $p = v^2/R$. Which one to use depends on what is known. If a fixed current flows through a resistor, dissipation grows with $R$; if a fixed voltage is applied across it, dissipation falls with $R$.

Example: 1.5 V across a 300 ohm resistor dissipates $1.5^2/300 = 7.5$ mW. A current of 10 mA through the same resistor dissipates $(0.01)^2 \cdot 300 = 30$ mW. On chip, $i^2R$ heating of wires drives self-heating and electromigration limits, and $v^2/R$ dissipation is the static cost of parallel terminations and resistive loads. A reliability checker therefore needs current densities, not just voltages, from the circuit engine.

## Going deeper

Alexander and Sadiku, "Fundamentals of Electric Circuits", chapter 1; Agarwal and Lang, "Foundations of Analog and Digital Electronic Circuits", chapter 1.

problems.q: A driver's output current ramps linearly from 0 to 40 mA over 8 ns and then stops. How much charge does it deliver during the ramp, in picocoulombs? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Charge is the integral of current: the area under a triangle, 40 mA times 8 ns over 2, which is 160 pC (one mA for one ns is one pC).

problems.q: A driver's output current ramps linearly from 0 to 13 mA over 8 ns and then stops. How much charge does it deliver during the ramp, in picocoulombs? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Charge is the integral of current: the area under a triangle, 13 mA times 8 ns over 2, which is 52 pC (one mA for one ns is one pC).

problems.q: A driver's output current ramps linearly from 0 to 30 mA over 12 ns and then stops. How much charge does it deliver during the ramp, in picocoulombs? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Charge is the integral of current: the area under a triangle, 30 mA times 12 ns over 2, which is 180 pC (one mA for one ns is one pC).

problems.q: A block draws a steady 35 mA from a 3.3 V supply for 75 ns. How much energy does it take from the supply, in picojoules? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Power is $P = VI = 3.3 \cdot 35 = 115.5$ mW, and energy is power times time: 115.5 mW for 75 ns is 8662.5 pJ.

problems.q: A block draws a steady 32 mA from a 1.2 V supply for 44 ns. How much energy does it take from the supply, in picojoules? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Power is $P = VI = 1.2 \cdot 32 = 38.4$ mW, and energy is power times time: 38.4 mW for 44 ns is 1689.6 pJ.

A current of 23 mA flows through a 60 ohm resistor. What power does the resistor dissipate, in milliwatts? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: $P = I^2 R = (23 \times 10^{-3})^2 \cdot 60$ W, which is 31.74 mW.

problems.q: A current of 9 mA flows through a 450 ohm resistor. What power does the resistor dissipate, in milliwatts? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: $P = I^2 R = (9 \times 10^{-3})^2 \cdot 450$ W, which is 36.45 mW.

label: Kirchhoff's current and voltage laws
lesson:
# Kirchhoff's current and voltage laws

Kirchhoff's two laws are the constraints every circuit simulator writes down before it solves anything. The current law says charge does not pile up at a node; the voltage law says potential is single-valued, so drops around any loop cancel. Nodal analysis, mesh analysis and the modified nodal analysis inside SPICE are all systematic ways to write these equations, so a tool builder must know exactly how many independent equations a network yields.

## Kirchhoff's current law at a node

Kirchhoff's current law (KCL) states that the currents leaving a node sum to zero at every instant: $\sum_k i_k = 0$, with entering currents counted negative. It is charge conservation applied to a node that stores no charge; any capacitance is modeled as a separate branch.

Example: at a node, 12 mA enters through branch 1, 5 mA leaves through branch 2 and 4 mA enters through branch 3. The net inflow is $12 - 5 + 4 = 11$ mA, so the fourth branch must carry 11 mA away from the node. If the arithmetic gives a negative number, that branch's current actually flows in. A simulator never chooses directions physically; it assigns a reference direction to every branch and lets the solution's sign report the truth.

## Kirchhoff's voltage law around a loop

Kirchhoff's voltage law (KVL) states that the voltage drops around any closed loop sum to zero. It follows from the electric field being conservative in lumped circuits: the potential at a point does not depend on the path taken to reach it. Walking around a loop, a source contributes a rise and each resistor a drop in the direction of its current.

Example: a loop holds a 3 V source and three elements dropping 0.8 V, 1.1 V and an unknown $V_x$ in the direction of the source's rise. KVL gives $3 = 0.8 + 1.1 + V_x$, so $V_x = 1.1$ V. A negative answer means the unknown element is actually a rise. KVL fails when changing magnetic flux threads the loop; then the loop's inductance must be modeled explicitly, which is why lumped models break at high frequency.

## Counting independent equations

A connected network with $n$ nodes and $b$ branches gives exactly $n - 1$ independent KCL equations: the $n$ node equations sum to zero, because every branch current leaves one node and enters another, so one equation is redundant. It gives $b - n + 1$ independent KVL equations: pick a spanning tree of $n - 1$ branches, and each of the remaining branches closes exactly one fundamental loop.

Example: 6 nodes and 9 branches give 5 independent KCL equations and $9 - 6 + 1 = 4$ independent loops. Together, $5 + 4 = 9$ equations match the 9 unknown branch currents once element laws relate currents and voltages. Nodal analysis picks the $n - 1$ node voltages as unknowns; mesh analysis picks the $b - n + 1$ loop currents. A simulator prefers nodal unknowns because they are easy to assign automatically and stay sparse.

## Going deeper

Desoer and Kuh, "Basic Circuit Theory", chapters 1 and 9; Chua, Desoer and Kuh, "Linear and Nonlinear Circuits", on graph-theoretic network equations.

problems.q: At a node, 4 mA enters through branch 1, 19 mA leaves through branch 2, 1 mA leaves through branch 3, 12 mA enters through branch 4. One more branch, branch 5, connects to the node. What current leaves the node through branch 5, in mA? A negative answer means the current actually enters.
problems.e: KCL says the currents leaving a node sum to zero, so branch 5 must carry away the net inflow of the other branches: -4 mA.

problems.q: At a node, 5 mA enters through branch 1, 13 mA enters through branch 2, 22 mA enters through branch 3, 15 mA enters through branch 4. One more branch, branch 5, connects to the node. What current leaves the node through branch 5, in mA? A negative answer means the current actually enters.
problems.e: KCL says the currents leaving a node sum to zero, so branch 5 must carry away the net inflow of the other branches: 55 mA.

problems.q: At a node, 2 mA leaves through branch 1, 8 mA leaves through branch 2, 24 mA leaves through branch 3. One more branch, branch 4, connects to the node. What current leaves the node through branch 4, in mA? A negative answer means the current actually enters.
problems.e: KCL says the currents leaving a node sum to zero, so branch 4 must carry away the net inflow of the other branches: -34 mA.

problems.q: A single loop contains a 3 V source and 2 elements in series with one unknown element. Going around the loop in the direction of the source's rise, element 1 drops 0.6 V, element 2 drops 1 V. What voltage drops across the unknown element, in volts? Round to 1 decimal place; a negative answer means a rise.
problems.e: KVL: the rise of the source equals the sum of the drops around the loop, so the unknown drop is $3 - 1.6 = 1.4$ V.

problems.q: A single loop contains a 2 V source and 2 elements in series with one unknown element. Going around the loop in the direction of the source's rise, element 1 drops 0.7 V, element 2 drops 0.3 V. What voltage drops across the unknown element, in volts? Round to 1 decimal place; a negative answer means a rise.
problems.e: KVL: the rise of the source equals the sum of the drops around the loop, so the unknown drop is $2 - 1 = 1$ V.

problems.q: A single loop contains a 4.5 V source and 2 elements in series with one unknown element. Going around the loop in the direction of the source's rise, element 1 drops 0.8 V, element 2 drops 0.6 V. What voltage drops across the unknown element, in volts? Round to 1 decimal place; a negative answer means a rise.
problems.e: KVL: the rise of the source equals the sum of the drops around the loop, so the unknown drop is $4.5 - 1.4 = 3.1$ V.

problems.q: A connected circuit has 5 nodes (counting the reference node) and 5 branches. How many independent KVL (loop) equations does it have?
problems.e: A spanning tree has 4 branches; each of the remaining $b - n + 1 = 5 - 5 + 1 = 1$ branches closes one independent loop.

problems.q: A connected circuit has 6 nodes (counting the reference node) and 14 branches. How many independent KCL equations does it have?
problems.e: The KCL equations of all 6 nodes sum to zero, so one is redundant: $n - 1 = 5$ are independent. The branch count does not matter.

problems.q: A connected circuit has 9 nodes (counting the reference node) and 12 branches. How many independent KVL (loop) equations does it have?
problems.e: A spanning tree has 8 branches; each of the remaining $b - n + 1 = 12 - 9 + 1 = 4$ branches closes one independent loop.

label: Series, parallel and divider networks
lesson:
# Series, parallel and divider networks

Series and parallel reduction and the divider rules are KCL and KVL applied to the two simplest topologies. They are the mental shortcuts behind effective drive resistance in timing, resistor-network reduction in extraction, and every quick sanity check an engineer runs on a simulator's answer. They also expose the first real engineering effect: a load changes the very voltage it is connected to.

## Series and parallel reduction

Resistors in series carry the same current, so their voltages add and $R_{eq} = R_1 + R_2 + \cdots$. Resistors in parallel share the same voltage, so their currents add and conductances add: $1/R_{eq} = 1/R_1 + 1/R_2 + \cdots$. For two in parallel, $R_1 \parallel R_2 = R_1 R_2/(R_1 + R_2)$, always below the smaller one.

Example: 100 ohm in series with the parallel pair of 300 ohm and 600 ohm. The pair is $300 \cdot 600/900 = 200$ ohm, so the total is 300 ohm. Network reduction in parasitic extractors repeatedly applies these rules, plus more general eliminations, to shrink millions of resistor segments into a small model. The rules hold only for elements that genuinely share a current or a voltage; bridges and meshes need nodal analysis.

## Voltage and current dividers

Two resistors in series across a source split its voltage in proportion to resistance: $V_{out} = V_s R_2/(R_1 + R_2)$ across $R_2$. Two resistors in parallel fed by a current split it in inverse proportion: the current in $R_1$ is $I R_2/(R_1 + R_2)$, so the smaller resistor takes the larger share.

Example: a 1.8 V source across 200 ohm on top and 400 ohm on the bottom gives $1.8 \cdot 400/600 = 1.2$ V at the midpoint. A 30 mA current entering 100 ohm in parallel with 200 ohm sends $30 \cdot 200/300 = 20$ mA through the 100 ohm branch. Both formulas follow from one KVL or KCL equation, and both are the building blocks of reference generation, level shifting and the effective-resistance estimates timers use for drivers.

## Loading a divider

A divider's output formula assumes nothing draws current from the midpoint. Connect a load $R_L$ across the bottom resistor and the bottom becomes $R_2 \parallel R_L$, which is smaller, so the output drops: $V_{out} = V_s (R_2 \parallel R_L)/(R_1 + R_2 \parallel R_L)$.

Example: 1 kohm over 1 kohm from 2 V gives 1 V unloaded. A 1 kohm load makes the bottom 500 ohm and the output $2 \cdot 500/1500 = 0.667$ V, a third lower. The error is small only when $R_L \gg R_2$. The same effect appears whenever a model is characterized under one load and used under another: a cell's delay measured into a light load, a reference voltage that sags when a block draws current. Engines that cascade stages must therefore carry the load forward, not assume it.

## Going deeper

Agarwal and Lang, "Foundations of Analog and Digital Electronic Circuits", chapter 2; Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics" (3rd ed.), chapter 1.

problems.q: A resistor of 60 ohm is in series with the parallel pair of 50 ohm and 60 ohm. What is the equivalent resistance, in ohms? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: The parallel pair is $50 \cdot 60/(50 + 60) = 27.27$ ohm; adding the series resistor gives 87.3 ohm.

problems.q: A resistor of 130 ohm is in series with the parallel pair of 480 ohm and 460 ohm. What is the equivalent resistance, in ohms? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: The parallel pair is $480 \cdot 460/(480 + 460) = 234.89$ ohm; adding the series resistor gives 364.9 ohm.

problems.q: A resistor of 200 ohm is in series with the parallel pair of 170 ohm and 260 ohm. What is the equivalent resistance, in ohms? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: The parallel pair is $170 \cdot 260/(170 + 260) = 102.79$ ohm; adding the series resistor gives 302.8 ohm.

problems.q: A 3.3 V source drives a divider: 450 ohm from the source to the output node, 80 ohm from the output node to ground. What is the output voltage, in volts? Round to 3 decimal places.
A current of 39 mA splits between two parallel resistors, 180 ohm and 20 ohm. How much current flows in the 180 ohm resistor, in mA? Round to 3 decimal places.
problems.e: The current divider sends the fraction $R_2/(R_1+R_2)$ through $R_1$: $39 \cdot 20/200 = 3.9$ mA.

problems.q: A current of 25 mA splits between two parallel resistors, 400 ohm and 400 ohm. How much current flows in the 400 ohm resistor, in mA? Round to 3 decimal places.
problems.e: The current divider sends the fraction $R_2/(R_1+R_2)$ through $R_1$: $25 \cdot 400/800 = 12.5$ mA.

problems.q: A divider of 110 ohm (top) and 340 ohm (bottom) is fed by 1.8 V. A load of 380 ohm is connected from the output to ground. What is the loaded output voltage, in volts? Round to 3 decimal places.
problems.e: The load parallels the bottom resistor: $340 \parallel 380 = 179.44$ ohm. Then $V_{out} = 1.8 \cdot 179.44/(110 + 179.44) = 1.116$ V, below the unloaded 1.36 V.

problems.q: A divider of 140 ohm (top) and 380 ohm (bottom) is fed by 1.8 V. A load of 420 ohm is connected from the output to ground. What is the loaded output voltage, in volts? Round to 3 decimal places.
problems.e: The load parallels the bottom resistor: $380 \parallel 420 = 199.5$ ohm. Then $V_{out} = 1.8 \cdot 199.5/(140 + 199.5) = 1.058$ V, below the unloaded 1.315 V.

problems.q: A divider of 20 ohm (top) and 340 ohm (bottom) is fed by 1.1 V. A load of 330 ohm is connected from the output to ground. What is the loaded output voltage, in volts? Round to 3 decimal places.
problems.e: The load parallels the bottom resistor: $340 \parallel 330 = 167.46$ ohm. Then $V_{out} = 1.1 \cdot 167.46/(20 + 167.46) = 0.983$ V, below the unloaded 1.039 V.

label: Nodal analysis
lesson:
# Nodal analysis

Nodal analysis chooses the node voltages as unknowns and writes KCL at every non-reference node. It is the method behind every SPICE-class simulator, because it can be assembled automatically from a netlist and produces a sparse, often symmetric, matrix. Solving two- and three-node networks by hand builds the intuition for what the simulator's matrix contains and why its structure matters.

## Writing one node equation

Pick a reference node (ground) and name the voltage of every other node relative to it. At each non-reference node, express every branch current leaving it in terms of node voltages, using $(V_a - V_b)/R$ for a resistor between $a$ and $b$, and add any current source. Then set the sum to zero.

Example: a 1.2 V source feeds node A through $R_1 = 2$ kohm; $R_2 = 4$ kohm runs from A to ground; a current source injects 0.3 mA into A. KCL at A: $(V - 1.2)/2 + V/4 = 0.3$. Multiplying out, $0.75V = 0.9$, so $V = 1.2$ V. Working in kohm and mA keeps the numbers in volts with no powers of ten. Every term has the form conductance times a voltage difference, which is what makes the method mechanical.

## Solving a two-node network

With two unknown nodes the KCL equations form a 2 by 2 linear system $G v = i$. The conductance matrix $G$ has the sum of conductances touching node $k$ on its diagonal and minus the conductance between nodes $j$ and $k$ off the diagonal; the right side holds source currents, including a voltage source seen through its series resistor as $V_s/R$.

Example: $V_s = 2$ V through 1 kohm to node 1, 1 kohm from node 1 to ground, 1 kohm from node 1 to node 2 and 1 kohm from node 2 to ground. In mS: $3V_1 - V_2 = 2$ and $-V_1 + 2V_2 = 0$. Then $V_1 = 2V_2$, so $5V_2 = 2$, $V_2 = 0.4$ V and $V_1 = 0.8$ V. Cramer's rule or elimination both work at this size; a simulator uses sparse LU.

## Three-node networks

A ladder of three nodes gives a tridiagonal 3 by 3 system: each node couples only to its neighbours. That sparsity is the norm in real circuits, where a node connects to a handful of others no matter how big the netlist, and it is why simulators scale to millions of nodes.

Example: a 3 V source drives 1 kohm to node 1, then 1 kohm to node 2, then 1 kohm to node 3, with 1 kohm from each node to ground. In mS the system is $3V_1 - V_2 = 3$, $-V_1 + 3V_2 - V_3 = 0$, $-V_2 + 2V_3 = 0$. Back-substituting $V_2 = 2V_3$ gives $V_1 = 5V_3$, and the first equation $15V_3 - 2V_3 = 3$ gives $V_3 = 0.231$ V, $V_2 = 0.462$ V, $V_1 = 1.154$ V. Gaussian elimination on a tridiagonal matrix costs linear time, the Thomas algorithm.

## Going deeper

Vlach and Singhal, "Computer Methods for Circuit Analysis and Design" (2nd ed.), chapters 2 and 3; Najm, "Circuit Simulation", chapter 2.

problems.q: A 3.3 V source connects through $R_1 = 1$ kohm to node A. Node A has $R_2 = 0.5$ kohm to ground and a current source injecting 1 mA into it. What is the voltage at node A, in volts? Round to 3 decimal places.

A 1 V source connects through $R_1 = 1$ kohm to node A. Node A has $R_2 = 10$ kohm to ground and a current source injecting 0.1 mA into it. What is the voltage at node A, in volts? Round to 3 decimal places.

A 1 V source connects through $R_1 = 8$ kohm to node A. Node A has $R_2 = 3$ kohm to ground and a current source injecting 0.7 mA into it. What is the voltage at node A, in volts? Round to 3 decimal places.

A 1 V source drives $R_1 = 10$ kohm into node 1. Node 1 has $R_3 = 6$ kohm to ground and $R_2 = 5$ kohm to node 2. Node 2 has $R_4 = 4$ kohm to ground. What is the voltage at node 1, in volts? Round to 3 decimal places.
problems.e: The node equations are $(G_1+G_2+G_3)V_1 - G_2 V_2 = G_1 V_s$ and $-G_2 V_1 + (G_2+G_4)V_2 = 0$, with $G = 1/R$ in mS. Solving gives $V_1 = 0.265$ V and $V_2 = 0.118$ V.

problems.q: A 1.1 V source drives $R_1 = 3$ kohm into node 1. Node 1 has $R_3 = 8$ kohm to ground and $R_2 = 3$ kohm to node 2. Node 2 has $R_4 = 0.5$ kohm to ground. What is the voltage at node 1, in volts? Round to 3 decimal places.
problems.e: The node equations are $(G_1+G_2+G_3)V_1 - G_2 V_2 = G_1 V_s$ and $-G_2 V_1 + (G_2+G_4)V_2 = 0$, with $G = 1/R$ in mS. Solving gives $V_1 = 0.493$ V and $V_2 = 0.07$ V.

problems.q: A 1.1 V source drives $R_1 = 6$ kohm into node 1. Node 1 has $R_3 = 6$ kohm to ground and $R_2 = 1.5$ kohm to node 2. Node 2 has $R_4 = 1$ kohm to ground. What is the voltage at node 1, in volts? Round to 3 decimal places.
problems.e: The node equations are $(G_1+G_2+G_3)V_1 - G_2 V_2 = G_1 V_s$ and $-G_2 V_1 + (G_2+G_4)V_2 = 0$, with $G = 1/R$ in mS. Solving gives $V_1 = 0.25$ V and $V_2 = 0.1$ V.

problems.q: A ladder: a 1.2 V source feeds 8 kohm to node 1, then 0.5 kohm from node 1 to node 2, then 1.5 kohm from node 2 to node 3. Nodes 1, 2 and 3 have 1, 1 and 1.5 kohm to ground. What is the voltage at node 1, in volts? Round to 3 decimal places.
problems.e: Writing KCL at each node gives a tridiagonal 3 by 3 conductance system. Its solution is $V_1 = 0.078$, $V_2 = 0.047$, $V_3 = 0.023$ V.

problems.q: A ladder: a 2.5 V source feeds 1 kohm to node 1, then 4 kohm from node 1 to node 2, then 3 kohm from node 2 to node 3. Nodes 1, 2 and 3 have 4, 10 and 4 kohm to ground. What is the voltage at node 3, in volts? Round to 3 decimal places.
problems.e: Writing KCL at each node gives a tridiagonal 3 by 3 conductance system. Its solution is $V_1 = 1.821$, $V_2 = 0.923$, $V_3 = 0.528$ V.

problems.q: A ladder: a 2.5 V source feeds 5 kohm to node 1, then 4 kohm from node 1 to node 2, then 0.5 kohm from node 2 to node 3. Nodes 1, 2 and 3 have 2.5, 5 and 10 kohm to ground. What is the voltage at node 2, in volts? Round to 3 decimal places.
problems.e: Writing KCL at each node gives a tridiagonal 3 by 3 conductance system. Its solution is $V_1 = 0.68$, $V_2 = 0.312$, $V_3 = 0.297$ V.

label: Modified nodal analysis and element stamps
lesson:
# Modified nodal analysis and element stamps

Plain nodal analysis cannot express an ideal voltage source or an inductor's DC short, so SPICE-class simulators use modified nodal analysis (MNA): node voltages plus selected branch currents as unknowns. The matrix is built element by element, each device adding a small pattern of entries called its stamp. Stamps are the interface between device models and the linear solver, which makes them the core data structure a simulator writer must master.

## Stamping conductances

A conductance $g$ between nodes $a$ and $b$ adds $+g$ to entries $(a,a)$ and $(b,b)$ and $-g$ to $(a,b)$ and $(b,a)$. A conductance from $a$ to ground stamps only $+g$ at $(a,a)$, because the ground row and column are deleted. Summing all stamps gives the nodal conductance matrix, which for a resistive network is a weighted graph Laplacian with the ground row removed: symmetric, diagonally dominant, and positive definite when every node has a path to ground.

Example: 1 kohm from node 1 to ground, 2 kohm between nodes 1 and 2 and 4 kohm from node 2 to ground. In mS: $G_{11} = 1 + 0.5 = 1.5$, $G_{22} = 0.5 + 0.25 = 0.75$ and $G_{12} = G_{21} = -0.5$. An entry between two nodes with no element between them is zero, which is where the sparsity comes from.

## Stamping voltage sources and inductors

An ideal voltage source fixes $V_a - V_b = E$ but does not say what current flows, so MNA adds its branch current $i_E$ as a new unknown. The stamp puts $+1$ and -1 in the new column at rows $a$ and $b$ (the current enters KCL there), and a new row $V_a - V_b = E$. An inductor is treated the same way, with its branch current as an unknown, which handles its DC short and its $v = L\,di/dt$ relation cleanly.

So the MNA system has one unknown per non-ground node plus one per voltage source and per inductor. Example: 11 nodes including ground, 3 voltage sources and 2 inductors give $10 + 3 + 2 = 15$ unknowns. Resistors, capacitors and current sources add no unknowns. The extra rows have zeros on the diagonal, so the matrix is no longer positive definite and the solver must pivot.

## Companion models for capacitors

In transient analysis the integration method turns each capacitor into a resistive companion model at every time step. Backward Euler approximates $i = C\,dv/dt$ by $i_n = (C/h)(v_n - v_{n-1})$: a conductance $G_{eq} = C/h$ in parallel with a current source $I_{eq} = (C/h) v_{n-1}$ that carries the history. The simulator stamps $G_{eq}$ like a resistor and $I_{eq}$ into the right-hand side, then solves a purely algebraic system.

Units on chip are convenient: femtofarads over picoseconds give millisiemens. Example: 100 fF at $h = 2$ ps gives $G_{eq} = 50$ mS; with $v_{n-1} = 0.6$ V the history source is 30 mA. Small steps make $G_{eq}$ large, which dominates the diagonal. Changing the step changes the matrix, which is why simulators refactor when they adapt $h$; the trapezoidal rule uses $2C/h$ with a different history term.

## Going deeper

Ho, Ruehli and Brennan, "The modified nodal approach to network analysis", IEEE Transactions on Circuits and Systems, 1975; Najm, "Circuit Simulation", chapters 2 and 4; the ngspice manual on transient analysis.

problems.q: A resistive network with ground as the reference node has 5 kohm between nodes 1 and 3, 4 kohm between nodes 2 and 3, 4 kohm from node 2 to ground, 5 kohm between nodes 1 and 2. In the nodal conductance matrix $G$ (rows and columns ordered by node 1, 2, 3), what is the entry $G_{22}$, in millisiemens? Round to 2 decimal places.

problems.e: Each conductance stamps $+g$ on the diagonals of its two nodes and $-g$ on the off-diagonal pair between them (a branch to ground stamps only its diagonal). Summing the stamps that touch entry (3, 2) gives -0.2 mS.

In the nodal conductance matrix $G$ (rows and columns ordered by node 1, 2, 3), what is the entry $G_{22}$, in millisiemens? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Each conductance stamps $+g$ on the diagonals of its two nodes and $-g$ on the off-diagonal pair between them (a branch to ground stamps only its diagonal). Summing the stamps that touch entry (2, 2) gives 0.7 mS.

In modified nodal analysis, where each voltage source and each inductor carries its branch current as an extra unknown, how many unknowns does the system have?
problems.e: Unknowns are the 15 non-ground node voltages plus one branch current per voltage source (2) and per inductor (2): 19. Resistors, capacitors and current sources stamp into existing rows.

In modified nodal analysis, where each voltage source and each inductor carries its branch current as an extra unknown, how many unknowns does the system have?

In modified nodal analysis, where each voltage source and each inductor carries its branch current as an extra unknown, how many unknowns does the system have?
problems.e: Unknowns are the 5 non-ground node voltages plus one branch current per voltage source (3) and per inductor (3): 11. Resistors, capacitors and current sources stamp into existing rows.

problems.q: A transient simulator discretizes a 120 fF capacitor with backward Euler at a time step of 5 ps. What conductance does the capacitor's companion model stamp, in millisiemens? Round to 3 decimal places.
problems.e: Backward Euler replaces $i = C\,dv/dt$ with $i_n = (C/h)(v_n - v_{n-1})$: a conductance $C/h = 120/5$ fF/ps, which is 24 mS.

problems.e: The companion model is a conductance $C/h = 25$ mS in parallel with a current source $(C/h) v_{n-1} = 25 \cdot 0.4 = 10$ mA.

problems.q: A transient simulator discretizes a 90 fF capacitor with backward Euler at a time step of 10 ps. The capacitor voltage at the previous step was 0.7 V. What is the magnitude of the history current source in its companion model, in mA? Round to 4 decimal places.
problems.e: The companion model is a conductance $C/h = 9$ mS in parallel with a current source $(C/h) v_{n-1} = 9 \cdot 0.7 = 6.3$ mA.

label: Mesh analysis
lesson:
# Mesh analysis

Mesh analysis is the dual of nodal analysis: it takes a current circulating in each window of a planar circuit as the unknown and writes KVL around each window. Simulators rarely use it, but it is the natural way to reason about loops, which is how inductance, return paths and current crowding are understood. It also shows how a shared element couples two unknowns.

## Writing a mesh equation

Assign a clockwise mesh current to each window of a planar circuit. Walking around a mesh in the direction of its current, each resistor contributes a drop of $R$ times the net current through it, and each source a rise or a drop depending on its polarity. For a single loop there is one unknown.

Example: a loop holds a 5 V source aiding the clockwise direction, a 2 V source opposing it, and resistors of 1 kohm and 2 kohm. KVL: $5 - 2 = (1 + 2) I$, so $I = 1$ mA. A source aiding the mesh current appears with a plus sign on the source side of the equation; an opposing one with a minus sign. Volts over kilohms give milliamperes, which keeps on-chip numbers readable.

## Solving two meshes

When two meshes share a resistor $R_3$, the current through it is the difference of the mesh currents. Writing KVL around each mesh gives a symmetric 2 by 2 system: the diagonal holds each mesh's total resistance and the off-diagonal holds minus the shared resistance:
$$(R_1 + R_3)I_1 - R_3 I_2 = V_1, \qquad -R_3 I_1 + (R_2 + R_3) I_2 = V_2,$$
with each $V$ the net source rise in its mesh's direction.

Example: $R_1 = 1$, $R_2 = 2$, $R_3 = 1$ kohm, a 4 V source aiding $I_1$, and a 1 V source aiding $I_2$. Then $2I_1 - I_2 = 4$ and $-I_1 + 3I_2 = 1$. Eliminating, $I_1 = 13/5 = 2.6$ mA and $I_2 = 1.2$ mA. The structure mirrors the nodal conductance matrix with resistances in place of conductances, and it stays symmetric because the shared resistor appears with the same sign in both equations.

## Branch currents from mesh currents

Mesh currents are fictitious loop variables; real branch currents are recovered from them. A branch on the outside of a single mesh carries that mesh's current. A shared branch carries the difference, $I_1 - I_2$ in the direction of $I_1$ when both meshes are clockwise.

Continuing the example with $I_1 = 2.6$ mA and $I_2 = 1.2$ mA, the shared 1 kohm resistor carries 1.4 mA in the direction of $I_1$ and drops 1.4 V. A sign error here is the most common mistake: the mesh currents cross a shared branch in opposite directions. This difference-of-loops picture is exactly how loop and partial inductances combine: the current in a shared return conductor is the sum or difference of the loop currents that use it, and its inductance couples those loops.

## Going deeper

Hayt, Kemmerly and Durbin, "Engineering Circuit Analysis", chapter 4; Desoer and Kuh, "Basic Circuit Theory", chapter 10.

label: Thevenin and Norton equivalents
lesson:
# Thevenin and Norton equivalents

Any linear network seen from two terminals behaves like one voltage source in series with one resistor (Thevenin) or one current source in parallel with one resistor (Norton). That equivalence is how timers model a driving gate, how extractors summarize a power grid seen from a pin, and how designers reason about loading without solving the whole network again.

## Open-circuit voltage

The Thevenin voltage $V_{th}$ is the voltage at the terminals with nothing connected. With the terminals open, no current flows into them, so any resistor in series with a terminal drops no voltage and can be ignored for this step.

Example: a 3 V source feeds $R_1 = 1$ kohm into node a, $R_2 = 2$ kohm runs from a to ground, and $R_3 = 5$ kohm runs from a to the output terminal. With the output open, $R_3$ carries no current, so the output sits at the divider voltage $3 \cdot 2/3 = 2$ V. In general $V_{th}$ comes from any method that solves the network with the terminals open: a divider, nodal analysis, or superposition over several sources.

## Thevenin resistance

The Thevenin resistance $R_{th}$ is the resistance seen looking into the terminals with every independent source zeroed: voltage sources replaced by shorts and current sources by opens. Dependent sources must stay, and then $R_{th}$ is found by applying a test source.

Continuing the example: shorting the 3 V source puts $R_1$ in parallel with $R_2$, $1 \parallel 2 = 0.667$ kohm, and $R_3$ is in series with that, so $R_{th} = 5.667$ kohm. A timer's driver model is this resistance in spirit: an effective resistance that charges the load. A strong driver has small $R_{th}$; a long series wire adds its resistance in series, which is why buffering a long wire helps.

## Norton current and maximum power transfer

The Norton equivalent replaces the source and series resistor by a current source $I_N = V_{th}/R_{th}$ in parallel with $R_{th}$; $I_N$ is the current that flows when the terminals are shorted. The two forms are interchangeable, and simulators convert between them when they stamp sources.

A resistive load $R_L$ draws power $V_{th}^2 R_L/(R_{th} + R_L)^2$, which peaks at $R_L = R_{th}$ with value $P_{max} = V_{th}^2/(4R_{th})$. Example: with $V_{th} = 2$ V and $R_{th} = 5.667$ kohm, $I_N = 0.353$ mA and $P_{max} = 4/22.67 = 0.176$ mW. Maximum power transfer is not maximum efficiency: at the matched point half the power is lost in $R_{th}$. The same matching idea, with impedances, returns in transmission-line termination.

## Going deeper

Agarwal and Lang, "Foundations of Analog and Digital Electronic Circuits", chapter 3; Alexander and Sadiku, "Fundamentals of Electric Circuits", chapter 4.

problems.e: Maximum power transfer happens at $R_L = R_{th} = 4.265$ kohm, giving $V_{th}^2/(4R_{th}) = 0.265^2/(4 \cdot 4.265) = 0.0041$ mW.

label: Capacitors and inductors as circuit elements
prereqs: Derivative as slope of tangent line
lesson:
# Capacitors and inductors as circuit elements

Capacitors and inductors are the elements that give circuits memory. A capacitor relates current to the rate of change of voltage, an inductor relates voltage to the rate of change of current. Every interconnect delay, every supply droop and every ground-bounce glitch comes from these two relations, and every transient simulator spends its time integrating them.

## Capacitor current from voltage slew

A capacitor stores charge $q = Cv$, so its current is $i = C\,dv/dt$. A constant voltage draws no current; a fast voltage ramp draws a large one. Integrating gives $v(t) = v(0) + \frac{1}{C}\int_0^t i\,dt$, so the voltage across a capacitor cannot jump unless infinite current flows.

Example: a driver slews a 20 pF load by 1.8 V in 0.6 ns. The current during the ramp is $20 \cdot 1.8/0.6 = 60$ mA (picofarads times volts per nanosecond is milliamperes). Multiply by the number of outputs switching together and the supply network must deliver amperes in nanoseconds, which is where decoupling capacitance and ground bounce come from. On chip, femtofarads and picoseconds give the same scaling.

## Inductor voltage from current slew

An inductor links magnetic flux $\lambda = Li$, and by Faraday's law the voltage across it is $v = L\,di/dt$. A steady current develops no voltage; a fast change in current does. Integrating, $i(t) = i(0) + \frac{1}{L}\int_0^t v\,dt$, so inductor current cannot jump.

Example: a current through a 3 nH bond wire changes by 40 mA in 0.5 ns. The induced voltage is $3 \cdot 40/0.5 = 240$ mV (nanohenries times milliamperes per nanosecond is millivolts). That voltage appears between the die's ground and the board's ground, which is ground bounce. Faster edges make it worse, because $di/dt$ grows as rise times shrink, so the packaging inductance becomes a timing and noise problem rather than a footnote.

## Stored energy

Charging a capacitor to $V$ stores energy $E = \frac12 CV^2$ in its electric field; a current $I$ in an inductor stores $E = \frac12 LI^2$ in its magnetic field. Both follow from integrating $p = vi$ with the element law.

Example: 10 pF at 1.2 V stores $0.5 \cdot 10 \cdot 1.44 = 7.2$ pJ. A 5 nH inductor carrying 100 mA stores $0.5 \cdot 5 \times 10^{-9} \cdot 0.01 = 25$ pJ. These energies explain two facts a power or reliability tool relies on. Charging a capacitor from a fixed supply through any resistance draws $CV^2$ from the supply: half is stored, half is dissipated in the resistance, which is the origin of the $CV^2 f$ dynamic-power term. And the energy stored in an inductor must go somewhere when its current is interrupted, which is the source of inductive voltage spikes.

## Going deeper

Agarwal and Lang, "Foundations of Analog and Digital Electronic Circuits", chapter 9; Rabaey, Chandrakasan and Nikolic, "Digital Integrated Circuits" (2nd ed.), chapter 5 on dynamic power.

label: RC circuits and time constants
prereqs: Capacitors and inductors as circuit elements
lesson:
# RC circuits and time constants

A resistor charging a capacitor is the most important waveform in digital design: every gate driving a wire and every wire charging a gate input is, to first order, an RC stage. The time constant $\tau = RC$ sets how fast it settles. Timers, delay calculators and reduced-order interconnect models all start from this exponential, so its formulas must be second nature to a tool builder.

## The time constant

KCL at the capacitor of a series RC driven by $V_s$ gives the first-order ODE $RC\,dv/dt + v = V_s$. Its natural response decays as $e^{-t/\tau}$ with time constant $\tau = RC$. On chip, kilohms times femtofarads give picoseconds, which makes mental arithmetic easy.

Example: a 2 kohm effective driver resistance into a 30 fF load gives $\tau = 60$ ps. When other resistors connect to the capacitor's node, the right $R$ is the Thevenin resistance seen by the capacitor with the sources zeroed. A source with 4 kohm series resistance driving a node that also has 4 kohm to ground and 50 fF gives $R_{th} = 4 \parallel 4 = 2$ kohm and $\tau = 100$ ps, not 200 ps. Forgetting the parallel path is a classic error in hand estimates.

## Charging and discharging waveforms

For a step from 0 to $V$ at $t = 0$ with the capacitor initially discharged, the solution is $v(t) = V(1 - e^{-t/\tau})$. A capacitor charged to $V$ and discharged through $R$ follows $v(t) = Ve^{-t/\tau}$. More generally $v(t) = v_\infty + (v_0 - v_\infty)e^{-t/\tau}$: final value plus the initial gap decaying exponentially.

Example: $\tau = 50$ ps and a 1 V step. At 50 ps the voltage is $1 - e^{-1} = 0.632$ V; at 100 ps, $1 - e^{-2} = 0.865$ V; at 150 ps, 0.950 V. After five time constants the gap is under 1%. The same formula covers discharge with $v_\infty = 0$: a 1 V node discharging with $\tau = 50$ ps is at 0.368 V after 50 ps. A simulator uses this closed form to check its integrator on a single RC, the simplest golden test of a transient engine.

## Time to cross a threshold

Delay is the time for the output to reach a threshold. Setting $1 - e^{-t/\tau} = f$ for a fraction $f$ of the final value gives $t = \tau \ln\frac{1}{1-f}$. For $f = 0.5$ this is $0.693\tau$; for 63.2% it is exactly $\tau$; for 90% it is $2.303\tau$; for 99% it is $4.605\tau$.

Example: $\tau = 80$ ps and a receiver that switches at 70% of the supply: $t = 80 \ln(1/0.3) = 80 \cdot 1.204 = 96.3$ ps. The threshold choice changes the number a lot, which is why libraries define delay at a stated threshold, usually 50%. The logarithm also shows a trap: chasing the last few percent of settling is expensive, so a timer that waits for full settling would be badly pessimistic.

## Going deeper

label: Rise time and 50 percent delay of an RC stage
lesson:
# Rise time and 50 percent delay of an RC stage

Timing libraries characterize every cell by two numbers per transition: the delay to the 50% point and the output transition time, usually measured between 10% and 90% (or 20% and 80%). For a single RC stage both are fixed multiples of $\tau$, and the rise time also sets the stage's bandwidth. These relations let a tool move between time-domain and frequency-domain views of the same edge.

## The 50 percent delay

For a step into a single RC stage, the output reaches 50% when $1 - e^{-t/\tau} = 0.5$, so $t_{50} = \tau\ln 2 \approx 0.693\tau$. This is the delay a timer would report for the stage if its input were an ideal step and the 50% points were used for delay measurement.

Example: a 4 kohm effective driver into a 25 fF load has $\tau = 100$ ps and $t_{50} = 69.3$ ps. Real inputs have finite slew, so library delays depend on input transition as well as load; the 0.69RC figure is the step-input limit. When a resistance and capacitance are distributed along a wire rather than lumped, the coefficient changes, which is the next concept's subject.

## The 10 to 90 percent rise time

The 10% point is at $\tau\ln(10/9) = 0.105\tau$ and the 90% point at $\tau\ln 10 = 2.303\tau$. Their difference is the 10-90 rise time, $t_r = \tau\ln 9 \approx 2.197\tau$. For a 20-80 measurement it is $\tau\ln 4 = 1.386\tau$.

Example: $R = 1$ kohm and $C = 200$ fF give $\tau = 200$ ps and $t_r = 439$ ps. The slew a timer propagates matters as much as the delay, because a slow input edge increases the next gate's delay and short-circuit current. Different libraries use different thresholds, so a delay calculator must convert slews with factors like $\ln 9/\ln 4 = 1.585$ between 10-90 and 20-80 conventions when it mixes data.

## Rise time and bandwidth

A single-pole low-pass $H(s) = 1/(1 + s\tau)$ has its 3 dB bandwidth at $f_{3dB} = 1/(2\pi\tau)$. Combining with $t_r = \tau\ln 9$ gives
$$t_r f_{3dB} = \frac{\ln 9}{2\pi} \approx 0.35.$$
So a rise time in picoseconds converts to bandwidth in gigahertz by $f_{3dB} \approx 350/t_r$.

Example: a 100 ps rise time corresponds to about 3.5 GHz of bandwidth. The rule ties together what a scope can resolve, what an interconnect model must represent, and how fast a buffer can drive a line. It is exact only for one real pole; systems with several poles or resonances have a different constant. A model fitted only up to 1 GHz cannot be trusted to reproduce a 50 ps edge, which needs about 7 GHz.

## Going deeper

Johnson and Graham, "High-Speed Digital Design: A Handbook of Black Magic", chapter 1; Rabaey, Chandrakasan and Nikolic, "Digital Integrated Circuits" (2nd ed.), chapter 4.

label: RLC circuits
prereqs: The roots of the characteristic equation
lesson:
# RLC circuits

Add inductance to an RC stage and the step response can ring. Series RLC behavior appears in package and bond-wire models, power-delivery networks, clock lines and long on-chip wires at high frequency. Its two parameters, the natural frequency and the damping ratio, decide whether an edge settles cleanly or overshoots, and they are the first thing a signal-integrity engine reports.

## Natural frequency and damping ratio

A series RLC with output across the capacitor obeys $LC\,v'' + RC\,v' + v = V_s$. The characteristic equation $LCs^2 + RCs + 1 = 0$ has roots set by two parameters: the undamped natural frequency $\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{LC}$ and the damping ratio
$$\zeta = \frac{R}{2}\sqrt{\frac{C}{L}} = \frac{R}{2\sqrt{L/C}}.$$
The quantity $\sqrt{L/C}$ is the circuit's characteristic resistance.

Example: $L = 4$ nH and $C = 1$ pF give $\sqrt{L/C} = \sqrt{4000} = 63.25$ ohm and $\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{4 \times 10^{-21}} = 1.58 \times 10^{10}$ rad/s, so $f_0 = 2.52$ GHz. With $R = 20$ ohm, $\zeta = 20/126.5 = 0.158$, strongly underdamped. Nanohenries over picofarads give $\sqrt{1000\,L/C}$ in ohms. Note that damping grows with $R$ in a series circuit; in a parallel RLC the roles flip and a larger $R$ means less damping.

## Critical damping

The roots are real and distinct when $\zeta > 1$ (overdamped: slow, no overshoot), repeated when $\zeta = 1$ (critically damped: fastest without overshoot) and complex when $\zeta < 1$ (underdamped: ringing at $\omega_d = \omega_0\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}$). Setting $\zeta = 1$ gives the critical resistance
$$R_{crit} = 2\sqrt{L/C}.$$

Example: a 2 nH package lead driving 2 pF has $\sqrt{L/C} = 31.6$ ohm, so $R_{crit} = 63.2$ ohm. A driver with less output resistance than that rings on this load. This is the lumped cousin of source termination on a transmission line, where the series resistance is chosen to match the line's characteristic impedance; in both cases the knob is a resistance compared with $\sqrt{L/C}$.

## Overshoot of an underdamped step

For $\zeta < 1$ the capacitor voltage after a unit step overshoots its final value. The peak occurs at $t_p = \pi/\omega_d$ and the fractional overshoot is
$$M_p = e^{-\zeta\pi/\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}}.$$
It depends only on $\zeta$: about 73% at $\zeta = 0.1$, 37% at $\zeta = 0.3$, 16% at $\zeta = 0.5$ and 4.3% at $\zeta = 0.707$.

Example: $L = 10$ nH, $C = 10$ pF and $R = 12.65$ ohm give $\sqrt{L/C} = 31.6$ ohm and $\zeta = 0.2$, so the overshoot is $e^{-0.2\pi/0.98} = 52.7$%. A 1 V edge peaks near 1.53 V, which can stress gate oxides and inject noise. Overshoot and ringing also cost timing, because the signal can cross the receiver threshold more than once. Signal-integrity checkers flag nets by exactly these metrics.

## Going deeper

Agarwal and Lang, "Foundations of Analog and Digital Electronic Circuits", chapter 12; Bakoglu, "Circuits, Interconnections, and Packaging for VLSI", chapter 6.

label: Distributed RC lines and wire delay
prereqs: Rise time and 50 percent delay of an RC stage
Heat equation and separation of variables
lesson:
# Distributed RC lines and wire delay

An on-chip wire is not one resistor and one capacitor; its resistance and capacitance are spread along its length. Modeled as a distributed RC line, its voltage obeys a diffusion equation, its delay grows with the square of length, and its 50% delay differs from the lumped estimate. These facts drive repeater insertion and every wire-delay model a placer or router uses.

## A wire as a distributed RC line

A wire of length $L$ with resistance $r$ and capacitance $c$ per unit length has totals $R = rL$ and $C = cL$. Cut into many small segments it becomes an RC ladder, and in the limit the voltage obeys $\partial v/\partial t = \frac{1}{rc}\,\partial^2 v/\partial x^2$, the heat equation. Signals diffuse rather than propagate.

The Elmore delay at the far end sums, for each element of capacitance $c\,dx$ at position $x$, the resistance between it and the driver, $rx$: $T = \int_0^L r x\, c\, dx = rcL^2/2 = RC/2$. Example: 1000 um of wire at 0.5 ohm/um and 0.2 fF/um has $R = 500$ ohm and $C = 200$ fF, so $RC = 100$ ps and the Elmore delay is 50 ps, half the lumped product, because the near-end capacitance sees little resistance.

## The 0.38 RC and 0.69 RC rules

Solving the diffusion equation for an ideal step at the near end gives a far-end 50% delay of about $0.38RC$, below the Elmore value $0.5RC$ (Elmore is an upper bound on the 50% delay of an RC tree's step response). A single lumped RC, with all resistance in front of all capacitance, gives $0.69RC$.

Example: the 500 ohm, 200 fF wire has $RC = 100$ ps; its 50% delay is about 38 ps, whereas lumping it would claim 69 ps. Lumped models therefore overestimate wire delay by nearly a factor of two. The 10-90 rise time of the distributed line is about $0.9RC$, against $2.2RC$ for the lumped stage. Practical delay calculators drive the wire with a driver resistance too, and then the total is close to $0.69R_dC + 0.38RC$ plus a cross term, which is why wire models are fitted rather than guessed.

## Quadratic growth with length

Because both $R$ and $C$ grow linearly with length, the wire's intrinsic delay grows as $L^2$: doubling a wire quadruples its delay. Splitting the wire into $k$ equal segments with ideal repeaters gives each segment $RC/k^2$, so the total wire delay is $k \cdot 0.38RC/k^2 = 0.38RC/k$, linear in length once the segment length is fixed.

Example: a 3000 um wire with $r = 0.4$ ohm/um and $c = 0.2$ fF/um has $RC = 1200 \cdot 600$ ohm fF $= 720$ ps and an unbuffered delay of about 274 ps. Three ideal repeaters' worth of segments cut the wire part to 91 ps. Real repeaters add their own delay, so an optimizer balances repeater delay against wire delay; the optimum segment length depends on the driver's resistance and input capacitance and on the wire's r and c.

## Going deeper

label: Phasors and sinusoidal steady state
prereqs: Capacitors and inductors as circuit elements
Exponential form of complex numbers (Euler's formula)
lesson:
# Phasors and sinusoidal steady state

In sinusoidal steady state every voltage and current in a linear circuit oscillates at the source frequency, differing only in amplitude and phase. Phasors capture those two numbers as one complex number, which turns differential equations into algebra. AC analysis in SPICE, S-parameter extraction and power-delivery impedance plots are all phasor computations, so phasor arithmetic is the working language of frequency-domain engines.

## Sinusoids as rotating complex numbers

Write $v(t) = V_m\cos(\omega t + \phi) = \mathrm{Re}\{V_m e^{j\phi} e^{j\omega t}\}$. The complex number $\mathbf{V} = V_m e^{j\phi}$, written $V_m\angle\phi$, is the phasor; the factor $e^{j\omega t}$ is common to every signal and is dropped. Differentiation becomes multiplication by $j\omega$, and adding same-frequency sinusoids becomes adding complex numbers.

Example: $3\cos(\omega t)$ plus $4\cos(\omega t + 90^\circ)$ mA. The phasors are 3 and $4j$, whose sum is $3 + 4j$ with magnitude 5 mA and angle $53.1^\circ$. Adding the amplitudes directly would give 7 mA, which is wrong unless the phases match. KCL and KVL hold for phasors exactly as they hold for instantaneous values, because they are linear.

## Element impedances

Substituting phasors into the element laws gives impedances, the ratio $\mathbf{V}/\mathbf{I}$: a resistor has $Z_R = R$, an inductor $Z_L = j\omega L$ and a capacitor $Z_C = 1/(j\omega C) = -j/(\omega C)$. Their magnitudes $\omega L$ and $1/(\omega C)$ are the reactances, with $\omega = 2\pi f$.

Example: at 100 MHz a 10 pF capacitor has $|Z_C| = 1/(2\pi \cdot 10^8 \cdot 10^{-11}) = 159.2$ ohm, and a 10 nH inductor has $|Z_L| = 2\pi \cdot 10^8 \cdot 10^{-8} = 6.28$ ohm. At 1 GHz those become 15.9 ohm and 62.8 ohm. A decoupling capacitor therefore looks like a short only at high enough frequency, and its own lead inductance eventually dominates, which is the whole story of power-delivery design: every capacitor is useful only over a band of frequencies.

## Phase between voltage and current

Because $\mathbf{I} = \mathbf{V}/Z$, the current's phase is the voltage's phase minus the impedance angle. Inductive impedances (positive angle) make current lag voltage; capacitive impedances (negative angle) make it lead.

Example: 100 ohm in series with 1 pF at 1 GHz. $1/(\omega C) = 159.2$ ohm, so $Z = 100 - 159.2j$ with angle $-57.9^\circ$. The current leads the source voltage by $\arctan(1/(\omega RC)) = \arctan(1.592) = 57.9^\circ$. At low frequency the capacitor dominates and the lead approaches $90^\circ$; at high frequency the resistor dominates and it approaches zero. Phase is what turns into delay and into the phase margin of feedback loops, so frequency-domain engines always report it with the magnitude.

## Going deeper

Agarwal and Lang, "Foundations of Analog and Digital Electronic Circuits", chapter 13; Nilsson and Riedel, "Electric Circuits", chapter 9.

label: Impedance and admittance
lesson:
# Impedance and admittance

Impedance generalizes resistance to sinusoidal steady state, and admittance is its reciprocal. With them, series and parallel rules, dividers, nodal analysis and Thevenin equivalents all carry over to AC with complex arithmetic. Frequency-domain simulators assemble a complex admittance matrix exactly the way DC analysis assembles a conductance matrix, so the same structural intuition applies.

## Series impedance magnitude

Impedances in series add. A series RLC has $Z = R + j(\omega L - 1/(\omega C))$, so
$$|Z| = \sqrt{R^2 + \left(\omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C}\right)^2}.$$
The inductive and capacitive reactances partly cancel, and at one frequency they cancel completely.

Example: $R = 20$ ohm, $L = 50$ nH and $C = 20$ pF at 200 MHz. $X_L = 2\pi \cdot 2 \times 10^8 \cdot 5 \times 10^{-8} = 62.83$ ohm and $X_C = 1/(2\pi \cdot 2 \times 10^8 \cdot 2 \times 10^{-11}) = 39.79$ ohm, so the net reactance is 23.04 ohm and $|Z| = \sqrt{400 + 530.9} = 30.51$ ohm. Below the cancellation frequency the circuit looks capacitive, above it inductive. A package lead plus decap is exactly this circuit, and its minimum impedance, equal to $R$, is what the decap buys.

## Admittance and parallel combinations

For parallel elements it is easier to add admittances, $Y = 1/Z$: a conductance $G = 1/R$, a capacitor $j\omega C$, an inductor $1/(j\omega L)$. Then $Z = 1/Y$. For a resistor in parallel with a capacitor, $Y = 1/R + j\omega C$ and
$$|Z| = \frac{R}{\sqrt{1 + (\omega RC)^2}}.$$

Example: 1 kohm in parallel with 10 pF at 100 MHz. $\omega RC = 2\pi \cdot 10^8 \cdot 10^3 \cdot 10^{-11} = 6.283$, so $|Z| = 1000/\sqrt{1 + 39.48} = 157.2$ ohm, close to the capacitor's own 159 ohm because it dominates. Frequency-domain MNA stamps $G + j\omega C$ into the same positions as the DC conductance, so an AC solve is a complex sparse solve per frequency point, with the same sparsity pattern at every frequency.

## Phase angle of an impedance

The angle of $Z = R + jX$ is $\theta = \arctan(X/R)$, positive for inductive and negative for capacitive impedance. It tells how far the current is shifted from the voltage, and it decides how much of the apparent power $|V||I|$ is real power, $|V||I|\cos\theta$.

Example: $R = 50$ ohm, $L = 10$ nH and $C = 100$ pF at 50 MHz. $X_L = 3.14$ ohm and $X_C = 31.83$ ohm, so $X = -28.69$ ohm and $\theta = \arctan(-28.69/50) = -29.8^\circ$: capacitive. The sign flips as frequency passes the point where the reactances cancel. A frequency sweep that plots $|Z|$ and $\theta$ together is how a power-integrity engineer reads a power-delivery network: magnitude says how much noise per ampere, phase says which element dominates there.

## Going deeper

Nilsson and Riedel, "Electric Circuits", chapters 9 and 10; Swaminathan and Engin, "Power Integrity Modeling and Design for Semiconductors and Systems", chapter 1.

label: Resonance and quality factor
lesson:
# Resonance and quality factor

At resonance the inductive and capacitive reactances of a circuit cancel. A series resonance makes impedance minimal; a parallel resonance makes it maximal. Both appear constantly in EDA: package and decap anti-resonances set power-delivery noise, clock and oscillator tanks set frequencies, and parasitic resonances in long nets cause ringing. The quality factor measures how sharp the resonance is.

## Resonant frequency

The reactances $\omega L$ and $1/(\omega C)$ are equal when $\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{LC}$, so the resonant frequency is
$$f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}.$$
At $f_0$ a series LC has zero net reactance, and a series RLC presents only $R$; a parallel LC has zero net susceptance and, ideally, infinite impedance.

Example: $L = 10$ nH and $C = 10$ pF give $LC = 10^{-19}$ s$^2$, $\sqrt{LC} = 3.16 \times 10^{-10}$ s and $f_0 = 503$ MHz. Quadrupling $C$ halves $f_0$. A useful shortcut: one nanohenry times one picofarad is $10^{-21}$ s$^2$, so $f_0 \approx 5033/\sqrt{L_{nH} C_{pF}}$ MHz; for 10 nH and 10 pF that is $5033/10 = 503$ MHz. Resonance is a property of the pair, so the same frequency appears whether the elements are wired in series or in parallel.

## Quality factor and bandwidth

For a series RLC, the quality factor is $Q = \omega_0 L/R = \frac{1}{R}\sqrt{L/C}$, the ratio of reactance at resonance to resistance. It equals $1/(2\zeta)$. The 3 dB bandwidth of the resonance is $\Delta f = f_0/Q = R/(2\pi L)$.

Example: $R = 2$ ohm, $L = 10$ nH and $C = 10$ pF. $\sqrt{L/C} = 31.6$ ohm, so $Q = 15.8$; with $f_0 = 503$ MHz the bandwidth is $R/(2\pi L) = 31.8$ MHz. Doubling $R$ halves $Q$ and doubles the bandwidth. At resonance, the voltage across the capacitor is $Q$ times the source voltage, so high-Q parasitic resonances amplify noise. A high Q is desirable in an oscillator tank and dangerous in a power-delivery network, where designers deliberately add damping.

## Anti-resonance in a power delivery network

Seen from the die, package inductance $L$ (with a small series resistance $R$) is in parallel with on-die decoupling capacitance $C$. This parallel tank has an anti-resonance near $f = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})$, where its impedance peaks. For high $Q$ the peak is
$$Z_{peak} \approx \frac{L}{RC} = Q^2 R.$$

Example: 0.5 nH of package inductance with 5 milliohm of resistance and 100 nF of decap. $f = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{5 \times 10^{-17}}) = 22.5$ MHz, $Q = \sqrt{L/C}/R = 0.0707/0.005 = 14.1$, and $Z_{peak} = 0.5 \times 10^{-9}/(0.005 \cdot 10^{-7}) = 1$ ohm. A 1 A current step with energy near that frequency would ring the supply by up to 1 V. Power-integrity tools sweep this impedance against a target impedance and add damping or more decap where it peaks.

## Going deeper

Swaminathan and Engin, "Power Integrity Modeling and Design for Semiconductors and Systems", chapters 1 and 2; Agarwal and Lang, "Foundations of Analog and Digital Electronic Circuits", chapter 14.

label: Linear time-invariant systems and convolution
lesson:
# Linear time-invariant systems and convolution

Linear time-invariant (LTI) systems are the reason circuit and interconnect analysis is tractable. Linearity lets responses superpose; time invariance lets one response be shifted to any time. Together they mean a system is fully described by its impulse response, and any output is a convolution. Reduced-order interconnect models, crosstalk superposition and waveform-based delay calculation all rest on this.

## Linearity and time invariance

A system is linear if scaling and adding inputs scales and adds outputs: input $a x_1 + b x_2$ gives output $a y_1 + b y_2$. It is time invariant if delaying the input by $T$ delays the output by $T$ and changes nothing else. RLC networks with fixed element values are LTI; transistors are not linear, which is why gate delays are tabulated rather than superposed.

Example: an interconnect model gives 0.4 V at $t = 30$ ps for input $x_1$ and 0.25 V at the same time for $x_2$. For input $3x_1 - 2x_2$ the output at 30 ps is $3 \cdot 0.4 - 2 \cdot 0.25 = 0.7$ V. Crosstalk analysis uses exactly this: the victim's waveform is the sum of its own response and the coupled responses from each aggressor, each computed separately.

## Discrete convolution

Any discrete input is a sum of scaled, shifted unit impulses, $x[n] = \sum_k x[k]\delta[n-k]$. By linearity and time invariance, the output is the same sum of scaled, shifted impulse responses:
$$y[n] = \sum_k h[k]\,x[n-k].$$
For finite sequences, only terms with both indices in range contribute.

Example: $h = [2, 1, -1]$ and $x = [1, 3, 2]$, both starting at $n = 0$. Then $y[0] = 2 \cdot 1 = 2$, $y[1] = 2 \cdot 3 + 1 \cdot 1 = 7$, $y[2] = 2 \cdot 2 + 1 \cdot 3 + (-1) \cdot 1 = 6$. The output length is $3 + 3 - 1 = 5$. Waveform engines that combine a sampled input with a sampled channel response compute exactly this sum, often with an FFT when the sequences are long, since direct convolution costs the product of the two lengths.

## Pulse response from the step response

A rectangular pulse of height $V$ from 0 to $T$ is a step of $V$ at $t = 0$ minus a step of $V$ at $t = T$. By superposition and time invariance, its response is the step response minus a delayed copy. For an RC stage with $s(t) = V(1 - e^{-t/\tau})$, after the pulse ends:
$$y(t) = V\left(e^{-(t-T)/\tau} - e^{-t/\tau}\right), \quad t > T.$$

Example: $\tau = 50$ ps, a 1 V pulse lasting 100 ps, observed at 150 ps: $y = e^{-1} - e^{-3} = 0.368 - 0.050 = 0.318$ V. During the pulse the output only reached $1 - e^{-2} = 0.865$ V. This decomposition is how glitch and noise propagation is analyzed: a narrow pulse may never reach a receiver's threshold, which is the basis of noise filtering in static noise analysis.

## Going deeper

Oppenheim and Willsky, "Signals and Systems" (2nd ed.), chapters 1 and 2; Lathi, "Linear Systems and Signals", chapter 2.

label: Fourier spectra of digital signals
prereqs: Rise time and 50 percent delay of an RC stage
lesson:
# Fourier spectra of digital signals

A digital signal is not a single frequency. Its spectrum, given by Fourier analysis, decides how much bandwidth every interconnect model, package model and measurement must cover. The harmonics of a clock, the knee frequency of an edge and the corners of a trapezoidal spectrum tell a tool designer what frequency range an extracted model must be accurate over, and where emissions will concentrate.

## Harmonics of a square wave

A periodic signal is a sum of harmonics at multiples of its fundamental $f_0 = 1/T$. An ideal 50% duty square wave from 0 to $V$ has a DC term $V/2$ and only odd harmonics, with amplitudes
$$c_n = \frac{2V}{n\pi}, \quad n = 1, 3, 5, \ldots$$
Even harmonics vanish because of the half-wave symmetry.

Example: a 1 V clock at 200 MHz has a 200 MHz component of $2/\pi = 0.637$ V, a 600 MHz component of 0.212 V and a 1 GHz component of 0.127 V, and nothing at 400 or 800 MHz. Amplitudes fall as $1/n$, slowly, so an ideal square wave has unbounded bandwidth. A duty cycle away from 50% brings the even harmonics back, which is one way emissions scans reveal a duty-cycle problem.

## The knee frequency

Real edges have finite rise time, which rolls off the high harmonics. A widely used rule of thumb from high-speed design places the knee frequency, below which most of an edge's energy lies, at
$$f_{knee} \approx \frac{0.5}{t_r},$$
with $t_r$ the 10-90 rise time. It is a guideline, not a theorem, and it is deliberately conservative relative to the 0.35/$t_r$ single-pole bandwidth.

Example: a 50 ps edge has $f_{knee} = 10$ GHz. A package or channel model that is accurate to 10 GHz will reproduce the edge's shape well; one fitted to 2 GHz will round the edge and miss reflections from small discontinuities. The clock frequency does not appear: a 100 MHz clock with 50 ps edges needs the same model bandwidth as a 2 GHz clock with 50 ps edges, which surprises people.

## The trapezoidal spectral envelope

A periodic trapezoidal pulse with pulse width $\tau$ and rise time $t_r$ has a spectral envelope with two corners. Below $1/(\pi\tau)$ the envelope is flat; between $1/(\pi\tau)$ and $1/(\pi t_r)$ it falls at 20 dB per decade; above $1/(\pi t_r)$ it falls at 40 dB per decade.

Example: a 5 ns pulse with 100 ps edges has corners at $1/(\pi \cdot 5 \text{ ns}) = 63.7$ MHz and $1/(\pi \cdot 100 \text{ ps}) = 3.18$ GHz. Halving the rise time moves the second corner to 6.37 GHz and raises every harmonic above the old corner by up to 6 dB. That is why electromagnetic compatibility problems often appear when a design is moved to a faster process without any change to its clock: the edges got faster. Emissions estimation tools use this envelope to bound spectra quickly.

## Going deeper

Paul, "Introduction to Electromagnetic Compatibility" (2nd ed.), chapter 3; Johnson and Graham, "High-Speed Digital Design: A Handbook of Black Magic", chapter 1; Ott, "Electromagnetic Compatibility Engineering", chapter 12.

label: Transfer functions and the Laplace domain
lesson:
# Transfer functions and the Laplace domain

The Laplace transform turns a linear circuit's differential equations into algebra in the complex frequency $s$. Each element becomes an impedance in $s$, and the ratio of output to input transforms is the transfer function $H(s)$. Model order reduction, AWE, Elmore delay, stability analysis and the initial and final value of any response all come from $H(s)$, which makes it the central object of interconnect analysis.

## Impedances in the s-domain

With zero initial conditions, a resistor's impedance is $R$, an inductor's is $sL$ and a capacitor's is $1/(sC)$. Circuits are then solved with the same divider, nodal and Thevenin rules as for resistors, but with rational functions of $s$. The DC gain is $H(0)$: capacitors become open circuits ($1/(sC) \to \infty$) and inductors become shorts ($sL \to 0$).

Example: $R_1 = 3$ kohm in series from input to output, and $R_2 = 1$ kohm in parallel with $C = 100$ fF to ground. At $s = 0$ the capacitor is open, so $H(0) = R_2/(R_1 + R_2) = 0.25$. Setting $s = j\omega$ recovers the phasor transfer function, so a Laplace-domain model gives both the transient and the frequency response.

## The pole of an RC divider

Continuing the network, the shunt arm is $Z_2 = R_2/(1 + sR_2C)$, and
$$H(s) = \frac{Z_2}{R_1 + Z_2} = \frac{R_2/(R_1 + R_2)}{1 + sC(R_1 \parallel R_2)}.$$
The single pole sits at $s = -1/\tau$ with $\tau = C(R_1 \parallel R_2)$: the capacitor sees the Thevenin resistance of the rest of the circuit.

Example: with $R_1 = 3$ kohm, $R_2 = 1$ kohm and $C = 100$ fF, $R_1 \parallel R_2 = 0.75$ kohm and $\tau = 75$ ps. The step response is $0.25V(1 - e^{-t/75\text{ ps}})$. Reading time constants off a transfer function's denominator is what a reduced-order model does: it keeps a few dominant poles and discards the rest. Here there is only one capacitor, so one pole is exact; a network with $n$ independent capacitors has $n$ poles.

## Initial and final values of a step response

For a step input $V/s$, the output transform is $Y(s) = H(s)V/s$. The final value theorem gives $y(\infty) = \lim_{s\to 0} sY(s) = H(0)V$ when the system is stable, and the initial value theorem gives $y(0^+) = \lim_{s\to\infty} sY(s) = H(\infty)V$.

Example: a probe attenuator has $R_1 \parallel C_1$ in the series arm and $R_2 \parallel C_2$ to ground. At high frequency the capacitors dominate, so $y(0^+) = V C_1/(C_1 + C_2)$; at DC the resistors dominate, so $y(\infty) = V R_2/(R_1 + R_2)$. With $C_1 = 10$ fF, $C_2 = 30$ fF, $R_1 = 3$ kohm and $R_2 = 1$ kohm, a 1 V step starts at 0.25 V and settles at 0.25 V: a flat response, because $R_1C_1 = R_2C_2$. Mismatched values give an overshooting or sagging edge, which is how a scope probe is compensated.

## Going deeper

Oppenheim and Willsky, "Signals and Systems" (2nd ed.), chapter 9; Pillage, Rohrer and Visweswariah, "Electronic Circuit and System Simulation Methods", chapters 2 and 3.

problems.q: A network has $R_1 = 8$ kohm in series from input to output, and $R_2 = 2.5$ kohm in parallel with $C = 170$ fF from output to ground. What is its DC gain $H(0)$? Round to 4 decimal places.

label: Poles, zeros and stability
prereqs: Transfer functions and the Laplace domain
lesson:
# Poles, zeros and stability

The poles of a transfer function are the natural frequencies of the system; the zeros are the frequencies it blocks. Pole locations decide stability, speed, damping and ringing. Model order reduction keeps the dominant poles, stability checks look for poles in the right half-plane, and passivity checks of extracted models start from the same picture.

## Poles as roots of the denominator

Write $H(s) = N(s)/D(s)$. The poles are the roots of $D(s)$ and the zeros the roots of $N(s)$. A real pole at $s = -p$ contributes a mode $e^{-pt}$ to the response, so its time constant is $1/p$. The pole closest to the origin decays slowest and dominates the response: it is the dominant pole.

Example: $D(s) = s^2 + 7s + 10$ with $s$ in units of $10^9$ per second factors as $(s + 2)(s + 5)$, poles at -2 and -5. The dominant pole -2 has a time constant of 0.5 ns. For $D(s) = s^2 + 4s + 13$ the roots are complex, $-2 \pm 3j$: the real part -2 sets the decay rate of the envelope and the imaginary part sets the ringing frequency, 3 Grad/s.

## Stability from pole locations

A linear system is stable when every pole has a negative real part: every natural mode then decays. A pole with positive real part grows without bound; a pole on the imaginary axis oscillates forever. For a quadratic factor $s^2 + bs + c$, if $c < 0$ the roots have opposite signs, one in the right half-plane; if $c > 0$ both roots lie in the half-plane where the sign of their real part equals the sign of $-b$.

Example: $(s + 3)(s^2 - 2s + 5)$ has one pole at -3 and two at $1 \pm 2j$: two right-half-plane poles, unstable. A passive RLC network can never have right-half-plane poles, so if a reduced-order interconnect model shows one, the reduction itself broke something. That check catches a real failure mode of moment-matching methods.

## Damping from pole positions

A complex pole pair $s = -\sigma \pm j\omega_d$ corresponds to a second-order factor $s^2 + 2\zeta\omega_n s + \omega_n^2$. The undamped natural frequency is the poles' distance from the origin, $\omega_n = \sqrt{\sigma^2 + \omega_d^2}$, and the damping ratio is $\zeta = \sigma/\omega_n$, the cosine of the angle the pole makes with the negative real axis.

Example: poles at $-3 \pm 4j$ (units of $10^9$ per second) give $\omega_n = 5$ and $\zeta = 0.6$, so the step overshoot is $e^{-0.6\pi/0.8} = 9.5$%. Poles at $-1 \pm 4j$ give $\omega_n = 4.12$ and $\zeta = 0.24$, much more ringing. Moving poles toward the imaginary axis lowers $\zeta$. Engineers read a pole plot geometrically: radius is speed, angle is damping.

## Going deeper

Franklin, Powell and Emami-Naeini, "Feedback Control of Dynamic Systems", chapter 3; Oppenheim and Willsky, "Signals and Systems" (2nd ed.), chapter 9.

problems.q: A transfer function has denominator $s^2 + 16s + 100$, with $s$ in units of $10^9$ per second. Its poles are a complex pair. What is their real part, in those units?
problems.e: $s = -8 \pm \sqrt{8^2 - 100} = -8 \pm j6$. The real part is half the negated linear coefficient, -8.

problems.q: A transfer function has denominator $s^2 + 11s + 10$, with $s$ in units of $10^9$ per second. What is the pole closest to the origin, in those units?
problems.e: The roots of $s^2 + 11s + 10$ are $s = -10$ and $s = -1$. The closer one, -1, is the dominant (slowest) pole.

problems.q: A transfer function has denominator $s^2 + 14s + 170$, with $s$ in units of $10^9$ per second. Its poles are a complex pair. What is their real part, in those units?
problems.e: $s = -7 \pm \sqrt{7^2 - 170} = -7 \pm j11$. The real part is half the negated linear coefficient, -7.

problems.q: A system's denominator factors as $(s + 5)(s^2 - 6 s + 9)$. How many of its poles lie in the open right half-plane?
problems.e: The first factor has its pole at $s = -5$. For $s^2 + bs + c$: if $c < 0$ the roots have opposite signs (one in the right half-plane); if $c > 0$ both roots share the sign of $-b$. Here that gives 2 right-half-plane pole(s) in total, so the system is unstable.

problems.q: A system's denominator factors as $(s + 2)(s^2 - s - 1)$. How many of its poles lie in the open right half-plane?
problems.e: The first factor has its pole at $s = -2$. For $s^2 + bs + c$: if $c < 0$ the roots have opposite signs (one in the right half-plane); if $c > 0$ both roots share the sign of $-b$. Here that gives 1 right-half-plane pole(s) in total, so the system is unstable.

problems.q: A system's denominator factors as $(s + 4)(s^2 + 5 s + 6)$. How many of its poles lie in the open right half-plane?
problems.e: The first factor has its pole at $s = -4$. For $s^2 + bs + c$: if $c < 0$ the roots have opposite signs (one in the right half-plane); if $c > 0$ both roots share the sign of $-b$. Here that gives 0 right-half-plane pole(s) in total, so the system is stable.

problems.q: A second-order system has poles at $s = -6 \pm j2$ (units of $10^9$ per second). What is its damping ratio $\zeta$? Round to 3 decimal places.
problems.e: $\omega_n$ is the poles' distance from the origin, $\sqrt{6^2 + 2^2} = 6.325$, and $\zeta = -\sigma/\omega_n = 6/6.325 = 0.949$.

problems.q: A second-order system has poles at $s = -9 \pm j14$ (units of $10^9$ per second). What is its undamped natural frequency $\omega_n$, in the same units? Round to 3 decimal places.
A second-order system has poles at $s = -9 \pm j14$ (units of $10^9$ per second). What is its damping ratio $\zeta$? Round to 3 decimal places.
problems.e: $\omega_n$ is the poles' distance from the origin, $\sqrt{9^2 + 14^2} = 16.643$, and $\zeta = -\sigma/\omega_n = 9/16.643 = 0.541$.

label: Bode magnitude and phase
lesson:
# Bode magnitude and phase

A Bode plot shows a transfer function's magnitude in decibels and its phase against log frequency. Because poles and zeros contribute straight-line asymptotes, a designer can sketch a response in seconds and read bandwidth, loop gain and phase margin off it. Frequency-response engines report these numbers, and model-fitting tools are judged by how well they reproduce them.

## Magnitude in decibels

Magnitude in decibels is $20\log_{10}|H|$ for voltage or current ratios (and $10\log_{10}$ for power ratios). Products of factors become sums in dB, which is why Bode plots add contributions. A single real pole $K/(1 + jf/f_p)$ has
$$|H|_{dB} = 20\log_{10}K - 10\log_{10}\left(1 + (f/f_p)^2\right).$$

Example: $K = 100$ and $f_p = 10$ MHz. The DC gain is 40 dB. At 10 MHz the exact gain is $40 - 10\log_{10}2 = 36.99$ dB, the familiar 3 dB point. At 30 MHz it is $40 - 10\log_{10}10 = 30$ dB. At 1 MHz it is $40 - 0.04 = 39.96$ dB. Each factor of 10 in voltage is 20 dB; a factor of 2 is about 6 dB. Power ratios use $10\log_{10}$, so a 3 dB power drop is the same point as a 3 dB voltage drop.

## Asymptotes of minus 20 dB per decade per pole

Far below a pole its factor is about 1 (0 dB); far above it falls as $f_p/f$, a straight line of -20 dB per decade. The asymptotes meet at $f_p$, where the true curve is 3 dB lower. For several real poles, above all of them the asymptotic magnitude is
$$|H|_{dB} \approx K_{dB} - \sum_k 20\log_{10}(f/f_{p,k}).$$
A zero contributes $+20$ dB per decade above its frequency.

Example: 80 dB DC gain with poles at 1 MHz and 100 MHz. At 1 GHz the first pole has taken $20\log_{10}1000 = 60$ dB and the second $20\log_{10}10 = 20$ dB, leaving 0 dB. Between the poles the slope is -20 dB per decade; beyond both it is -40. The asymptotic error is largest near each corner and at most 3 dB per isolated pole.

## Phase of poles and zeros

A real left-half-plane pole contributes phase $-\arctan(f/f_p)$: 0 well below it, $-45^\circ$ at the pole and $-90^\circ$ well above. A left-half-plane zero contributes $+\arctan(f/f_z)$. The phase of a product is the sum of the phases, so
$$\angle H = -\sum_k \arctan(f/f_{p,k}) + \sum_m \arctan(f/f_{z,m}).$$

Example: poles at 1 MHz and 10 MHz, evaluated at 3 MHz: $-\arctan 3 - \arctan 0.3 = -71.6^\circ - 16.7^\circ = -88.3^\circ$. Phase changes over about two decades around each pole, so it starts moving well before the magnitude does. That spread is what limits feedback: by the time a loop's gain has fallen to 1, the extra poles have already eaten into the phase.

## Going deeper

Sedra and Smith, "Microelectronic Circuits" (8th ed.), appendix F on Bode plots; Franklin, Powell and Emami-Naeini, "Feedback Control of Dynamic Systems", chapter 6.

An amplifier has $H(f) = 87/(1 + jf/f_p)$ with $f_p = 2$ MHz. What is its exact gain at 6 MHz, in dB? Round to 2 decimal places.
An amplifier has $H(f) = 66/(1 + jf/f_p)$ with $f_p = 5$ MHz. What is its exact gain at 100 MHz, in dB? Round to 2 decimal places.
A transfer function has a DC gain of 50 dB and real poles at 2 MHz and 200 MHz. Using the straight-line Bode asymptotes, what is the magnitude at 2000 MHz, in dB? Round to 2 decimal places.

problems.e: Each pole subtracts 20 dB per decade above its frequency: $50 - 20\log_{10}(100/1) - 20\log_{10}(100/10) = -10$ dB.
